The use of the term as propaganda, as a pejorative term for liberal Democrats, does not constitute an evolution in meaning. If we based our language on the language of propaganda, it would be impossible to speak about anything without affirming the view implied by the terms - in this case, that Bernie Sanders' political views lie outside the range of views that can realistically be implemented in America (because he's a "socialist," and we all know socialists have no place here).

Also, you are incorrect in claiming that Bernie Sanders is a democratic socialist - he isn't, because he does not advocate for government ownership of the means of production. Whether this is a failing on your part to retain the correct definition of democratic socialism, or you're simply ignorant of Sanders' platform, I cannot say. But it is plainly false; he is no kind of socialist.

The evolution of the term isn't due to the pejorative usage; it's due to the rise of "social democracy" in Europe, which has given rise to its proponents being called socialists rather than the more accurate but longer and more difficult to say "social democrats."

Again, you're technically correct that the proper definition of a socialist is one who advocates state ownership of the means of production, but the term has strayed from that usage at this point, much like the term "liberal" no longer refers to the same kinds of liberals it did 200 years ago.

Well, that initial point may be true, and it may not; I don't see you offering any evidence for it, which suggests that you take it to be self-evident (which is essentially the party line). Whether this is "just" semantics, or not, I think the words we use and their implied meanings are important and relevant to the thread. The article itself is largely about the language and framing used to discuss Bernie Sanders in mainstream media.

Semantics, in this sense, are actually the medium of a great deal of political strategy. "How can we frame this guy, whose platform serves the interests of most American workers, as a threat to American workers?" Well, calling him a socialist is a great way to do that; makes him sound like a goddam Commie! But calling him an advocate for social democracy..."Hmmm...hey what is this social democracy anyway?"

If they didn't call it socialism, relatively uneducated working Americans might actually go and find out what his platform was (because they wouldn't just have the knee-jerk anti-socialism reaction). And in fact, social democracy is very appealing to non-elite Americans. You can find polling data saying Americans reject "socialism," but also that they support having the government invest in new infrastructure, raising minimum wages, providing for old people who lack resources, and so on.

Fair enough, but I suspect that it's less an intentional campaign to delegitimize him and more a result of what sets him apart from the establishment. Because he's the social democrat to Clinton's neo-liberal, he gets called a socialist by comparison. It's a similar phenomenon to people calling Rand Paul a libertarian even though he isn't one, because he's closer to a libertarian than the rest of the Republican party.

All this being said, I can see the potential for negative connotations and spin, so I'll avoid calling Sanders a socialist in the future.
